summary:
San Luis Potosí stands within the national framework of Mexico, where legal gender recognition remains the unfinished core of LGBTQ+ equality. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of Mexico's 32 states had legislated a legal gender-recognition procedure by that date, and set out a state-by-state compliance picture showing that implementation differs sharply from one state to another. Where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

San Luis Potosí is among the states that have legislated. The state began authorizing legal gender changes for transgender people on 17 May 2019, under a 2019 reform of the Civil Registry Law that created an administrative recognition procedure, with implementing regulations issued by gubernatorial decree.

Partnership and family rights are in place on the same timeline. Same-sex marriage took effect in the state on 21 May 2019, after the state Congress voted 14-12 in favour on 16 May 2019, and joint adoption by same-sex couples has been legal in the state from the same month. Nationally, same-sex marriage has been legal since 2009.

Two further statutory features shape the protection picture. San Luis Potosí appears among the Mexican states whose hate-crime statutes recognise motivation by gender and sexual preference, and its local anti-discrimination law bans discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender, but not on the ground of gender identity. The omission of gender identity from that statute leaves a gap in the ordinary discrimination remedy available to trans residents.

No state-specific evidence of enforcement practice, incidents or local ordinances was found, and no border-screening or identity-document procedure specific to San Luis Potosí is recorded. Visitors should therefore expect the statutory position as described, without a sourced indication of how recognition requests are processed in practice.
tangentialFactors:
The gap between statute and practice recurs across Mexico. Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) concludes that the country's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice; the analysis explicitly cautions that it must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

Violence against trans people intensified over the year to mid-2024. AP reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City; the killings drew LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the preceding twelve months. Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to Brazil's 100.

Delays and refusals in name and gender recognition have documented consequences. The Human Rights Watch report "I Just Want to Contribute to Society" (6 March 2024) found that in Tabasco trans residents are left carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying everyday discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police, set against killings including a trans woman found dead in the Carrizal River in August 2023.

Legislative and inter-American responses have targeted the same failures. Mexico City's Congress approved the "Paola Buenrostro law" in July 2024, criminalising transfemicide, a statute named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that all LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.
localsOnly:
Residents of San Luis Potosí can request a legal name and gender change through the administrative procedure created by the 2019 Civil Registry Law reform, with the procedure's implementing regulations fixed by gubernatorial decree rather than by further legislation.

The state's anti-discrimination statute covers sexual orientation and gender as protected grounds but omits gender identity, so a discrimination complaint framed explicitly around gender identity has no direct statutory basis in that law. Hate-crime sentencing provisions in the state, by contrast, recognise gender and sexual-preference motivation as aggravating factors.

Same-sex couples have been able to marry in the state since 21 May 2019 and to adopt jointly from the same month. The state Congress approved the marriage reform by a 14-12 margin on 16 May 2019.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether San Luis Potosí's recognition procedure is functioning, how long processing takes, and whether refusals or delays occur are not sourced in the available material; the Human Rights Watch backgrounder of 31 March 2025 sets out a per-state compliance picture, but the specific findings for San Luis Potosí are not reproduced here.

No source in the inventory records immigration or border-screening practices that could expose a visitor's trans status on entry to Mexico or at the state's ports of entry, and no state-specific record of document-issuance practice exists for San Luis Potosí.

Whether the state's hate-crime statute's reference to "gender" motivation has been applied to anti-trans attacks in San Luis Potosí, and whether any prosecutions for such attacks have occurred, is unresolved. No incidents of violence against trans people in the state are documented in the available sources.

Whether the state's gender-identity law has been amended since 2019, and whether the omission of gender identity from the anti-discrimination statute has been addressed by any later reform, is not sourced.
